item.content:encoded:
Braves' Walt Weiss provides update on Chris Sale NLDS plan appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Atlanta Braves have been meticulous in how they handle Chris Sale for the last three years, making sure to give him enough rest so that he can maintain his excellent form for an entire campaign. The 2024 National League Cy Young Award winner has still spent time on the injured list, but their plan has helped him become a top-tier starting pitcher once again. All bets are off in the playoffs, though. Right?
Two days after starting Game 1 of the NL Wild Card Series versus the Philadelphia Phillies, Sale made it clear he wanted to take the mound in a do-or-die Game 3. Despite holding a 6-2 lead in the eighth inning, manager Walt Weiss brought in the veteran left-hander to finish off Atlanta's longtime rival. Sale indicated that he still plans to pitch against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday night, but nothing is official yet.
In fact, it sounds like there is serious doubt surrounding the 10-time All-Star's status for Game 2 of the NL Division Series. Although Weiss said a Sale start in LA is "still on the table," the Braves want their ace to be fresh enough for postseason battle.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"We're gonna err on the side of giving him (time to rest) if it's even close," the NL Manager of the Year candidate revealed, per ESPN's Alden Gonzalez. That statement is a far cry from Sale's confident remarks following Atlanta's series-clinching win over Philly. Weiss has been in baseball a long time, however.
It is possible the skipper is just engaging in some good old-fashioned gamesmanship before his squad faces the two-time reigning World Series champions. The Braves are a title contender in their own right, but they will want to gain a mental edge on the Dodgers if one is attainable. Disarming the home team with a surprise pitching move seems like the perfect gambit to try in October. Dave Roberts is a veteran of this game as well, though, so he may not be caught off guard.
Of course, there is a possibility that Walt Weiss is merely telling the truth. Perhaps Atlanta will wait until it returns to Truist Park to start Chris Sale. If so, then the team's bullpen move in Game 3 of the Wild Card round will seem even more puzzling.
One thing is for certain. Sale is a warrior who has openly expressed his desire to carry a big workload in the playoffs. We shall see if the Braves trust him to run wild in Chavez Ravine. The time for speculation will soon end. Game 1 of the NLDS begins on Saturday at 4 p.m. ET.

The win has to feel great for Braves fans, who saw that same Phillies team eliminate them in the 2022 and 2023 NLDS'. As for what is up next, the team will be taking on the high-powered Los Angeles Dodgers in the 2026 NLDS. Atlanta's starting rotation is admittedly quite thin at t
item.content:encoded:
After not winning a postseason series since their 2021 World Series championship, the Atlanta Braves got back in the playoff win column in 2026 with a 2-1 Wild Card series win against their rival Philadelphia Phillies.
The win has to feel great for Braves fans, who saw that same Phillies team eliminate them in the 2022 and 2023 NLDS'. As for what is up next, the team will be taking on the high-powered Los Angeles Dodgers in the 2026 NLDS.
Atlanta's starting rotation is admittedly quite thin at the moment, with only three starting pitchers currently healthy. Those arms are lefty Chris Sale and right-handers Tyler Mahle and Grant Holmes.
Sale, their ace, threw a total of 116 pitches during the Wild Card series, 21 of which coming on Thursday night. The Braves are in Los Angeles for games 1 and 2 on Saturday and Sunday, which complicates matters.
Sale will likely not be ready for Game 2 on Sunday on what is essentially two days' rest. David Vassegh of MLB Network reported Friday that manager Walt Weiss would not commit to Sale starting Sunday, and also said starters Martín Pérez and Bryce Elder will not be on the NLDS roster.
Walt Weiss wouldn’t commit to Chris Sale starting Game 2 on Sunday.
Weiss also said Bryce Elder and Martin Perez won’t be available for NLDS. #Dodgers #Braves
— David Vassegh (@THEREAL_DV) October 2, 2026
Game 1's starter has yet to be announced either, and if Sale cannot get Game 2 then perhaps it would Mahle or Holmes. The Braves are really going to have to get creative in order to give their bats a chance to win this series.
Throughout the regular season, the club gave the 37-year-old Sale ample rest between outings, usually at least five or six days and sometimes more. The hope is for that schedule to possibly have made him fresher for the postseason.
An interesting wrinkle that may have developed during that Wild Card for the Braves was the emergence of lefty long reliever Ray Kerr. He threw 47 pitches on Thursday while keeping the Phillies scoreless.
He could likely open one of the early games in the series, or at least give some innings out of the bullpen. As for Sale, he could theoretically be ready to go for Tuesday's Game 3 in Atlanta on full rest.
This story was originally published by Athlon Sports on Oct 2, 2026, where it first appeared in the MLB section. Add Athlon Sports as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

item.title: [FanSided] MLB Power Rankings: Every remaining playoff team after Wild Card Round
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline

item.content:encoded:
With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts.
The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. As for Braves-Dodgers? Well, there's plenty of recent history there. But which teams have the look of title contenders as we move deeper into October? Let's rank all eight remaining teams in terms of championship equity.
8. Chicago White Sox
The White Sox made it hard on themselves down the stretch, but Chicago is riding high after a first-round sweep of the Astros, with blessings from the Pope. Coming into the postseason, the White Sox were broadly dinged for their youth and inexperience. As fate would have it, though, the South Siders were significantly more poised than a seasoned Astros team.
Chicago's lineup performed top to bottom. They worked deep into counts and made smart, situational swings. The rotation is still a mess, and the bullpen is not much better, but there's a lovable underdog quality to this White Sox team that is hard to ignore. By default, the White Sox rank last here, but an ALDS matchup with the Guardians is perfectly winnable. Do not discount the possibility of a South Siders pennant run.
7. Cleveland Guardians
Cleveland has been there and done that. This team is always the AL Central champ, it feels like, even when the odds are stacked against them. The Guardians hit much better down the stretch after a brutal start to the campaign, while their pitching is a potential superpower. Parker Messick and Gavin Williams can match just about any aces blow-for-blow, and this bullpen always tends to perform.
The question now becomes: Can Stephen Vogt's squad translate their signature Guards Ball style to October? The answer for years now has been "no." Cleveland lacks thump in the heart of the order, but tends to execute the small things — bunts, base-running, two-strike hitting — better than anyone. Chicago's pitching staff is vulnerable and the Guardians have the edge in experience, but so did Houston. And the Astros' bats were much better. The outcome of this series will not shock me in either direction, to be frank.
6. Atlanta Braves
The Braves lineup struggled down the stretch but appeared to wake up against the Phillies, especially in the clincher. Atlanta has no shortage of offensive talent and a deep bullpen, with plenty of postseason experience to draw on. So why ranked so low?
Well, the rotation is a mess. Chris Sale is an elite 1A, but Tyler Mahle is questionable against better offensive teams (see: Dodgers) and their third starter is Grant Holmes behind an opener. Atlanta has seven starters on the IL and could struggle to build a bridge to the stellar back end of their bullpen in non-Sale starts. That said, if the Braves' bats heat up, perhaps it does not matter. There is a clear break in quality between Cleveland at No. 7 and the rest of the field. The Braves are very, very capable of mounting a deep run. Atlanta notably went 5-1 against the Dodgers this season.
5. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays just kept winning all season long. There was no more consistent force in the American League. We can quibble with the back half of their lineup and question the depth of their rotation, but the Rays are an extremely disciplined club with star power (Junior Caminero) and fundamental skills (Chandler Simpson, Jonny DeLuca) in equal measure.
Tampa is going to defend at a high level and run the bases with intent. Their pitching staff does not look so fearsome on paper, but Drew Rasmussen is a bonafide ace and Freddy Peralta looked more like himself in September. Whether this team can match the raw explosiveness of the Yankees' lineup is the swing factor. On the flip side, New York has a propensity for unforced errors that Tampa can ruthlessly capitalize on.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees are still waiting on Aaron Judge. New York stuffed its Wild Card roster with platoon bats and situational hitters, but Aaron Boone probably needs more pitchers for a five-game Divisional Series. The lineup exploded against the Red Sox, but Tampa will almost certainly manage its pitching staff better than Chad Tracy and Boston did.
New York is the best team in the American League on paper, even with all their injuries, but the bullpen is perilously thin and it's hard to trust this lineup completely. Ben Rice has caught fire at an optimal moment, so there's that. And the Yankees boast, by far, the most star power of any team west of Los Angeles. Whether it can all come together against a healthy, well-rested Rays team remains to be seen.
3. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers, almost without fail, dominate the regular season despite ownership's pervasive cheapness. This team knows how to develop talent in-house and locate value on the margins. There is no better-run small-market clubhouse in MLB. And yet, Milwaukee has consistently fallen flat in the playoffs. Whether or not this year is any different comes down to a couple factors.
First, Jacob Misiorowski helps. Milwaukee has the best pitcher in baseball and he may damn near guarantee a Game 1 win in the NLDS. The Brewers' bullpen is rock solid, too, while the depth of their rotation is respectable. Milwaukee's pitching can win ballgames. More importantly, there's less elite competition than usual; even the Dodgers are scuttling at the plate, while the entire American League is poked full of holes. The path has never been clearer for the Brewers, who compensate for limited slug with impressive plate discipline and savvy situational hitting. If Milwaukee can maintain its extraordinarily high baseline, there's reason to believe this could be the year it all clicks.
2. San Diego Padres
There are few stars I trust more in a high-leverage spot than Fernando Tatis Jr. The man just makes good things happen, whether he's using his power or his speed. San Diego's entire lineup, really, has come on strong in the final month. After sputtering for much of the regular season, the likes of Jackson Merrill and Manny Machado have apparently remembered how talented they are. Gavin Sheets and Ty France are improbably major contributors. On the pitching front, Michael King and Nick Pivetta tore through a loaded Cubs lineup. The Padres' bullpen is the best in baseball, so no team can more easily build a bridge between their frontline starters and the ninth inning.
San Diego's rotation depth is suspect; once Walker Buehler and Robbie Ray are asked to carry several innings, it could get dicey. But in terms of momentum and top shelf star power, the Padres clear the majority of the competition around them. It can't hurt that San Diego plays the Dodgers as well as any team, either. That matchup could ultimately define the 2026 season, assuming the Padres can out-slug the No. 1 seed Brewers.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
This shouldn't come as a shock. The Dodgers aren't as untouchable as their reputation suggests, but there's still only one team with Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow lined up on the mound. Meanwhile, Shohei Ohtani has proven his capacity for clutch swings time after time since arriving in Hollywood two years ago. Los Angeles has the best pitchers and the best player in MLB, with a star-studded lineup to boot. Mookie Betts, Kyle Tucker and Freddie Freeman weren't at the peak of their powers this season, but that's still a group worth trusting when every at-bat is magnified.
Los Angeles has depth, too. Josue De Paula is one of the most exciting young bats in baseball and the Dodgers barely have room for him on the roster. Alex Call and Dalton Rushing are useful as situational hitters. The primary concern is L.A.'s bullpen, but Rōki Sasaki, Kris Bubic and Justin Wrobleski — their excess rotation arms — should help the Dodgers cover innings when needed. The Dodgers are banged-up and very much vulnerable, but this is still the team to beat, full stop.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Braves' Chris Sale matches his own rare MLB postseason feat
item.dc:creator: Matt Wadleigh
item.description: Chris Sale got things started for the Atlanta Braves by starting Game 1 against the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round. item.content:encoded:
Chris Sale got things started for the Atlanta Braves by starting Game 1 against the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round.
Sale finished the series against the Phillies as well.
The Braves won on Thursday night, 6-2, but it was Sale who pitched the final 1.1 innings for Atlanta to end the game and send them to the NLDS against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
As it turns out, Sale is the first pitcher to throw both the first and last pitches for his team in a postseason series since 2018. The other one to do it in 2018? It was Chris Sale himself, when he was with the Boston Red Sox.
Chris Sale of the @Braves is the first MLB pitcher to throw both the first and last pitches for his team in a postseason series since he himself did so in the 2018 World Series. pic.twitter.com/7esVOkXBlT
— OptaSTATS (@OptaSTATS) October 2, 2026
In 2018, Sale started Game 1 of the World Series against the Dodgers, although he went just four innings and allowed three runs as the Red Sox won 8-4.
Sale then pitched the final inning of Game 5 as the Red Sox won the World Series.
Here was the scene from Thursday night.
Chris Sale sends the @Braves to the NLDS! #CLINCHED
(MLB x @BudweiserUSA) pic.twitter.com/gaa66CiYCy
Exactly one week ago, the @RedSox finished their most dominant season. pic.twitter.com/nqYzeKI0LD
— MLB (@MLB) November 5, 2018
Braves manager Walt Weiss used a total of six pitchers on Thursday night in a win-or-go-home scenario, and Sale threw 21 pitches to keep Atlanta's season alive.
The Braves face the Dodgers on Saturday in Game 1 and Sunday in Game 2, and it will be interesting to see when Sale gets his next start.

item.title: [MLB.com] Sale's pitch to Weiss pays off: Lefty bookends Braves' Wild Card Series win
item.dc:creator: Paul Casella
item.description: The Braves' ace had an important matter to address before Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series on Thursday night at Truist Park. "First of all, I was not going to go to Chris Sale and ask him if he could pitch tonight," Weiss said after the Braves’ series-clinching 6-2 win. item.content:encoded:
The Braves' ace had an important matter to address before Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series on Thursday night at Truist Park.
"First of all, I was not going to go to Chris Sale and ask him if he could pitch tonight," Weiss said after the Braves’ series-clinching 6-2 win. "I didn't want to put him in that position, because I knew that, even if he was hanging, he would tell me yes. So I was not going to bring it up."
Turns out, Weiss didn't need to.
"Literally as soon as I stepped in my office this afternoon, he was sitting in the chair across from my desk," Weiss said. "And he looked at me and he said, 'I feel amazing.'”
Weiss’ response?
“Well, let's talk."
From there, the two laid out a plan that ultimately saw Sale take down the final four outs of the Braves' first postseason series win since the 2021 World Series. Keep in mind, Sale also recorded the club's first 19 outs of this Wild Card Series as the Game 1 starter in Atlanta's 5-3 victory two days earlier.
In doing so, Sale became the first pitcher to start Game 1 of a postseason series and finish off that same series since ... Chris Sale. He previously did the same thing for the Red Sox in the 2018 World Series against the Dodgers.
Sale joined Clayton Kershaw as the only pitchers to accomplish the feat multiple times in postseason history.
"What a warrior, man," Weiss said. "This guy -- I've run out of superlatives for Chris Sale. Been talking about him all year. He's one of the best I've ever been around."
Even with Sale’s mid-afternoon ambush opening up some options for Weiss, their meticulously crafted plan only worked if all of the pieces fell into place.
Ray Kerr had to go out and do his job as the opener. Grant Holmes had to take it from there and relay the torch to a trio of relievers -- Robert Suarez, Didier Fuentes and Dylan Dodd -- who each had to take care of business.
And even then, the offense also needed to do its part. Michael Harris II checked that box early with a three-run homer in the first inning, then Ozzie Albies (a two-run shot in the fourth) and Matt Olson (a solo blast in the seventh) tacked on.
"Unbelievable. I'm just thankful for the opportunity, honestly," Sale said. "This could not be more of a group effort. This was basically a culmination of our entire year. All hands on deck. Everyone is doing everything they can to just get a win for this team."
Safe to say everything went to plan?
Well, sort of.
Knowing the plan was to pitch against the top of the Phillies' order in either the eighth or the ninth inning, Sale started to throw in the bullpen in the top of the seventh. But when Olson's homer extended the Braves' lead to 6-1 in the bottom of the seventh, it altered the strategy.
Even with Philadelphia's 9-1-2 hitters due up, Weiss instead went with the left-handed Dodd to start the eighth. He gave up a leadoff triple to pinch-hitter Derek Hill, who then scored on Trea Turner's sacrifice fly to cut the lead to four.
Needing to face at least three batters, Dodd had to stay in to face Kyle Schwarber -- the same guy who homered in the eighth inning off Dylan Lee one day earlier to trigger the Phillies' Game 2 comeback. Dodd was up to the task, though, getting MLB's regular-season home run leader to fly out for the second out.
Then, it was showtime: Sale vs. Bryce Harper.
"Electric," Harris said of the moment Sale emerged from the bullpen.
"The best," Albies said. "The minute I saw him getting warmed up, I said, 'He's definitely coming in. I love this.' The energy, the excitement there -- everybody was pumped that he came in the game."
Well, everyone except the Phillies.
Sale struck out Harper on four pitches, getting him to chase three sliders well out of the zone. The last one missed badly enough to go to the backstop, but catcher Drake Baldwin tracked it down to throw out Harper.
Now came another decision for Weiss: Let Sale go back out for the ninth or turn it over to closer Raisel Iglesias with a four-run lead?
With Iglesias warming just in case, the home crowd roared as Sale emerged from the dugout to trot back out for the ninth. Four batters later, the Braves had punched their ticket for an NLDS showdown with the Dodgers.
"Was hoping he only had to go one," Weiss said, "but he had to get to four outs."
All told, Sale -- the Braves' presumed starter for Sunday's Game 2 -- threw 21 pitches over 1 1/3 innings.
Is he still good to go for Sunday?
"I don't know. I have no idea," Weiss said. "We weren't even worried about that. It was just, 'Put this thing down and then we'll have those conversations later.' But yeah, we haven't even talked about that. It was all about tonight."
If Weiss has any doubts, he’ll certainly be getting another visit this weekend at Dodger Stadium.
"If I had to pitch tomorrow," Sale said, "I'd pitch tomorrow."

item.content:encoded:
Atlanta Braves left-hander Chris Sale, who finished the game himself even before the fatigue of his first start, expressed his feelings.
Sale expressed his feelings about winning in an interview after beating the Philadelphia Phillies 6-2 in Game 3 of the wild-card series at Truist Park in Atlanta, Georgia on the 2nd (Korea time).
Two days after starting Game 1, he took the mound with two outs in the eighth inning and secured the last four outs to confirm his team's series victory, saying, "This is why we play baseball."
He first showed his respect for the opposing Phillies. "Dave Dombrowski is the boss he was with in Boston. It's a really great front desk, and it's someone to go to the Hall of Fame. Manager Don Mattingly is one of the most respected people in baseball. Among the players, there are many Hall of Fame players. I pay my respects to them. I really respect the team," he said, showing courtesy to the opponent.
"When you meet a respected opponent, the joy of the game increases," he continued, adding, "I think this is the beauty of baseball, that we came this far head-on with such a strong team."
He continued with emotion. "This is why we play baseball. It doesn't make sense if you don't feel excited about such a game, or if you don't enjoy that our game today is the only game in the wild-card series that went to Game 3. This is what baseball is like. What we do, this fierce game, is baseball itself."
He also said, "It's not easy for us to enjoy a moment like this. Some people never enjoy this kind of joy throughout their careers. So of course you will enjoy this moment. We are well aware that there is still work to be done. We have to enjoy this moment and prepare for the next game," he added.
Manager Walt Weiss said, "Today I didn't ask him to take the mound. He said, "I tried not to talk about it because I would say I can do it if I ask," adding, "Sale's appearance on the day was hurt."
"I went to the supervisor's office this afternoon and he was sitting on the chair in front of my desk. And he looked at me and said, 'I feel amazing today.' So we started a conversation. I began to plan. He said he would use it if he had to face the top lineup in the eighth or ninth inning. The plan worked out as planned. I wanted to throw only one inning, but I caught four outs," he said, explaining the situation.
Colleagues were also enthusiastic about Sale's appearance. Michael Harris II said, "It was really thrilling," and the moment he saw the sale coming out of the bullpen, Ozzy Albies also said, "Seeing him warming up, I thought, 'I'm sure he'll take the mound.' It was a wonderful moment. It was great energy and heat. When he came out, everyone was encouraged," he said, recalling the time.
This is not the first time for Sale. In 2018, when he was a member of the Boston Red Sox, he also started Game 1 and finished the game in Game 5. According to "Opta STATS," Sale is the only record to set such a record since 2018.
Weiss said, "He's a warrior. I don't know what more praise to give. He's the best player I've ever been with. He praised the ace, saying, "As a teammate, I am the best in everything, including my temperament as a matchmaker, my performance, and my sincere attitude."
Now the question is next. After a day off, they will play the division series against the Los Angeles Dodgers. Weiss said, "I don't know yet. I haven't worried about that part," he said, declining to comment.
Sale was full of confidence. "If you tell me to throw it tomorrow, I'll do that," he said. I will do everything," he said, raising his voice.
[Atlanta (USA) = KIM JAE HO, MK Sports Correspondent]

item.title: [nbcphiladelphia.com] Phillies' season ends with the pain of another early postseason knockout
item.dc:creator: Jim Salisbury
item.description: ATLANTA – While the Phillies tried to extend their season Thursday night against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, their Delta 757 charter sat 23 miles away at Hartsfield-Jackson International airport. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – While the Phillies tried to extend their season Thursday night against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, their Delta 757 charter sat 23 miles away at Hartsfield-Jackson International airport.
A win would send the Phillies west, to Los Angeles and a second straight National League Division Series matchup with the Dodgers.
A loss would send them home, to Philadelphia and another long, cold winter.
It didn’t take long to figure out which way the Phillies would be heading. Aaron Nola was tagged for three runs in the first inning. The Phillies never recovered. Their season came to an end in a 6-2 loss to the Braves in Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series.
For just the second time in franchise history, the Phillies qualified for the postseason for a fifth straight year, matching a team-high streak first reached from 2007 to 2011. The Phils won the World Series in 2008, but have not since. They made a surprising run to the World Series in 2022 but were beaten by the Houston Astros in six games. They were a win away from returning to the World Series in 2023 only to collapse and lose Games 6 and 7 of the NL Championship Series at home to Arizona. Since then, they have gone the wrong way, losing in the Division Series (their first round of play) in 2024 and 2025 and now in the Wild Card Series.
“It’s always frustrating,” Kyle Schwarber said in the quiet of the losing clubhouse. “From every postseason I’ve been in, it always hurts when you’re not the last team standing.
“It’s just as frustrating this year as it was last year and the year before that.”
Philadelphia Phillies
Complete coverage of the Fightin' Phils and their MLB rivals from NBC Sports Philadelphia.
As the October defeats have mounted, the team’s core group of high-priced veteran players has gotten older.
Schwarber, always the optimist, insisted that the team’s championship window is still wide open. So did J.T. Realmuto, saying, “There’s definitely the talent in this room to win. If you watched us play all year, no matter who we played, we weren’t outmatched. It’s about execution. It’s not about the age and the years. We know we still have the talent to win.”
Over on the other side of the clubhouse, Bryce Harper didn’t sound so sure.
He was asked what gives him faith that the team can still get to where it wants to go.
“Yeah, I don’t know,” he said. “It’s going to be a long offseason, obviously. I have trust in the organization and the people that are in charge. We’ll see where we go.”
Heading into the offseason, the Phils have many questions, first and foremost: Will Don Mattingly return as manager in 2027? He took over, with an interim tag, for Rob Thomson after the team got off to a 9-19 start in April.
The Phillies played .590 ball (79-55) under Mattingly, but president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski tried to hire Alex Cora when he let Thomson go, and he seems likely to try again in the coming weeks. Stay tuned.
Mattingly would not touch the topic after the game. Schwarber, Realmuto, Nola and Trea Turner all said they’d like to see Mattingly return. Harper declined to talk about the topic.
If Cora comes on board, he will be taking over a team of highs and lows, one with an inconsistent offense that is seemingly up one month (see August) and down the next (see September). He will be taking over a team that lacks pitching depth, both in the starting rotation and the bullpen. Both weaknesses reared their head in recent weeks as the Phils had to scramble to make the playoffs, using ace Zack Wheeler on the final day of the regular season, a circumstance that prevented him from starting Game 1 of the postseason.
Wheeler mentioned the team’s overall inconsistency when asked if he believed the Phils still had the talent to make a deeper postseason run next year.
“Consistency in every group, I think that’s what will get us there,” he said. “We were kind of inconsistent throughout the year. Maybe we were hitting, but we weren’t pitching well. Maybe we were pitching well and we weren’t hitting well. We just have to put it all together throughout the majority of the season.
“We’re hungry, that’s for sure. We just didn’t get the job done.”
The Phils had chances to win the series.
Jesus Luzardo pitched well in Game 1 and they held a 3-2 lead in the seventh. With few trusted arms in his leaky bullpen, Mattingly went to his All-Star closer, Jhoan Duran, in the bottom of the seventh. Duran got through that inning but gave up the lead on a three-run homer in the eighth and the Phillies lost, 5-3.
They bounced back to win a wild Game 2 Wednesday in 10 innings on the strength of three late home runs and the clutch pitching of Cristopher Sanchez, Alex McFarlane and Andrew Painter. They seemed to have momentum heading into Game 3.
But the momentum disappeared quickly as Nola had big trouble throwing strikes.
Just three of the right-hander's first 13 pitches to open the game were strikes. He fell behind Ronald Acuna Jr., and Matt Olson, the Braves’ Nos. 2 and 3 hitters, with 3-0 counts and eventually walked both. He then fell behind Michael Harris II, 2-0. Harris hit the next pitch, a sinker down and out of the zone, over the right-field wall for a three-run homer.
“I think he was just a little too careful,” Realmuto said of Nola. “I don’t think he was way off because he was just missing. They just did a good job of not chasing and making him come in the zone. When a lineup is good like that and they get on a roll, it’s tough to get them out when they’re not chasing.”
Nola did not make it through the second inning. Tim Mayza got the final out of the frame before handing off to Wheeler in the top of the third. The Phillies’ brain trust opted not to start Wheeler on three days’ rest. He'd never done that before. Also, Wheeler admitted that at this point of the season, he wasn’t feeling 100 percent. It was decided that Nola’s best chance of succeeding would be to stay in a starter’s role.
“We’re going to need Nola in this game,” Mattingly said before the game. “Starting him gives us the best version of him.”
The Phillies weren’t sure Wheeler would even be able to pitch until he tested himself by playing catch before the game. He ended up pitching four innings but was not particularly sharp. He gave up three hits and walked three. One of those walks turned into a run when Ozzie Albies stroked a two-run homer in the fourth to give the Braves a 5-0 lead.
“We felt Nola was on solid rest,” Mattingly said after the game. “If he could get us into the game at all, we’d have Zack after that. Obviously, it didn’t go well.”
Atlanta used lefty Ray Kerr as an opener. He pitched 3 1/3 innings and did not allow a run. The only hit Kerr gave up was a single to Schwarber in the first inning. Kerr then struck out Harper.
Grant Holmes, Robert Suarez, Didier Fuentes, Dylan Dodd and Chris Sale finished off the Phillies. Sale, the Braves’ ace lefty who started Game 1, entered with two outs in the eighth and struck out Harper.
Before the 2019 season, Harper signed a 13-year, $330-million contract with the Phillies. He came looking for a parade down Broad Street. Eight years later, he boarded a flight back to Philadelphia, still looking.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] MLB playoff predictions 2026: Expert picks for every ALDS, NLDS series
item.dc:creator: Daniel Mader

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff predictions 2026: Expert picks for every ALDS, NLDS series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
October has officially arrived, just in time for the MLB postseason to ramp up.
With all four Wild Card series now over — three of which ended in two-game sweeps — just eight teams remain alive in the pursuit of a World Series title, with the Guardians, Rays, Dodgers and Brewers entering the picture after watching the first round from home.
Some of baseball's biggest stars, from Shohei Ohtani and Jacob Misiorowski to Junior Caminero and Cam Schlittler, will be on full display for the division series. On both sides of the bracket, the question will be whether the teams carrying their Wild Card momentum can now take down a well-rested heavyweight.
With a chance to reset between rounds, the best-of-five ALDS and NLDS matchups begin Saturday. Who will advance to the championship series?
With Wild Card matchups in the rearview mirror, The Sporting News predicts the 2026 MLB division series matchups.
MORE: Complete MLB playoff schedule for 2026 postseason
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 2 Cleveland Guardians
You can certainly debate whether the Guardians (85 regular-season wins) or White Sox (84 regular-season wins) really belong on the postseason stage this season, with neither AL Central squad owning a ton of big-name star power. Regardless, the fact is that Cleveland and Chicago both find themselves with an opportunity to make a serious postseason run in a weaker AL bracket — and the White Sox have already taken advantage.
Chicago enters the ALDS the momentum of its first postseason series win since the 2005 World Series, proving in the Wild Card round that it has the power and pitching depth to challenge opponents. Cleveland, though, has better top-end starting pitching in Parker Messick, Gavin Williams and Tanner Bibee.
These two teams are well familiar with each other; the White Sox won the season series, 7-6. Cleveland's offense isn't very threatening, ranking last among all postseason teams in team OPS (.696) — this matchup will likely come down to how early the White Sox's bats can get to Guardians starters.
Saturday will mark the first time in MLB history that the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland have met in the postseason.
The White Sox began playing baseball in 1894 as the Sioux City Cornhuskers.
The Guardians began playing baseball in 1896 as the Columbus Buckeyes/Senators.
The fact that this is a divisional matchup means it will likely be close, but Chicago's momentum is hard to ignore, and there was only a one-win discrepancy between the sides in the regular season. The White Sox are finally building something serious, seemingly with a new hero every night. The power in Will Venable's lineup is dangerous enough to reach the ALCS.
Prediction: White Sox in 4
No. 4 New York Yankees vs. No. 1 Tampa Bay Rays
It's been clear since the start of the postseason that whichever AL East team emerged from the lower half of the bracket would be favored to reach the World Series. This is the heavyweight matchup of the two ALDS series, featuring elite starting pitching on both sides and some of MLB's premiere sluggers.
Of course, the massive question lingering over this matchup is how much, if at all, Aaron Judge will play for the Yankees. Even as the lower seed, if he's near 100 percent, it's hard not to view New York as the favorite to reach the ALCS; a healthy Judge, alongside Cody Bellinger, Luis Garcia Jr. and Ben Rice, takes Aaron Boone's lineup to a new level, capable of matching the all-around offensive excellence of Tampa Bay's quartet: Caminero, Yandy Siaz, Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson.
The Rays won this season series 7-6, but it may be the most evenly matched division series. Both sides can roll out a trio talented starters — New York with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Gerrit Cole, and Tampa Bay with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and Shane McClanahan — to pair with deep offenses.
Yankees can line up their pitching as follows against the Rays:
Game 1: Gerrit Cole
Game 2: Cam Schlittler
Game 3: Max Fried
Game 4: Gerrit Cole
Game 5: Cam Schlittler
For two reasons, the Yankees are the pick here. For one, between Schlittler and arguably the best bullpen in baseball, New York is loaded with leverage arms. And the Yankees are also riding high off a dominant Wild Card series, biding time for Judge and Giancarlo Stanton to heal. Assuming those two sluggers can at least be used in some key at-bats, the Yankees' lineup is capable of changing games in an instant.
Prediction: Yankees in 5
No. 3 Atlanta Braves vs. No. 2 Los Angeles Dodgers
The Dodgers' path to becoming the first National League team to win three-straight World Series will begin with a matchup against a 94-win Braves squad fresh off a Wild Card win over the Phillies.
Los Angeles' rest advantage could be significant. Even if he's not pitching, Ohtani has been dealing with lingering injury concerns over the last few months. A week off between his last regular season game should only benefit him, not to mention the Dodgers' ability to line up their loaded starting rotation however they choose. With the Braves using Chris Sale in two games against Philadelphia, he may not be available early in the NLDS.
The Dodgers and Braves have built quite the postseason history. 👀🔥
2013 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2018 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2020 NLCS — LAD def. ATL
2021 NLCS — ATL def. LAD
2026 NLDS — ??? 🤔 pic.twitter.com/mHhbDO9gDX
The top of Atlanta's lineup is potent enough to make this an interesting series, and the team did beat the Dodgers five times in the regular season, but Ronald Acuna Jr., Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies will have to meet the moment in the NLDS. Yoshinobu Yamamoto has pitched well against Atlanta in his career, as have Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow.
Even if the Braves' bats can keep things close, it's hard to imagine Atlanta's pitching staff beyond Sale being able to contain Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Kyle Tucker and Mookie Betts over a five-game series. The Braves are a good team, but the Dodgers are far too talented to fall this early in the bracket.
Prediction: Dodgers in 4
No. 4 San Diego Padres vs. No. 1 Milwaukee Brewers
This matchup pins baseball's best team all season, Milwaukee, against one of its hottest over the past month, San Diego. While the Brewers are the clear favorites here, between the best starting pitcher in the game this season and a deep lineup that plays to contact, the Padres do pose some interesting challenges, going 4-2 against Milwaukee in the regular season.
On one hand, San Diego has stars made for October. As shown in the Wild Card round, when the top of the Padres' lineup is on, they're a hard team to beat — Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado, Xander Boegarts, Ty France and Jackson Merrill can look like one of the best 1-through-5 groups in baseball at times. Add in an elite starter (Michael King) and a strong bullpen led by Mason Miller, and there's a path for the Padres to pull off a stunner here.
Most data has shown that the more of a threat a team is to hit the ball out of the yard, the better they'll fare in the postseason. If this is finally going to be the year the Brewers reach a World Series — putting an end to their cycle of regular season success with playoff shortcomings — they'll need to slug more. This is an offense that's outstanding at making contact and getting on base, but has also continually come up short in October and finished second-to-last in team home runs (154) in the 2026 regular season.
Chances are, Milwaukee won't only be able to rely on its strong pitching staff to reach the World Series. The Brewers' bats will need some extra-base hits. But with the Padres' lackluster starting pitching depth, this is still a series the Brewers can claim even if they're not pristine.
San Diego may have some top-end talent and momentum, but the Padres can't match Milwaukee's all-around depth.
Prediction: Brewers in 4

item.title: [cbssports.com] Braves' Chris Sale: Closes out Wild Card Series
item.dc:creator: RotoWire Staff
item.description: Sale pitched 1.1 scoreless innings to close out Atlanta's victory over Philadelphia in Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series on Thursday. He allowed one hit and no walks while striking out three. Sale threw 95 pitches during Atlanta's Game 1 win, and he returned to the mound only two days later to eliminate the division-rival Phillies. item.content:encoded:
Sale pitched 1.1 scoreless innings to close out Atlanta's victory over Philadelphia in Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series on Thursday. He allowed one hit and no walks while striking out three.
Sale threw 95 pitches during Atlanta's Game 1 win, and he returned to the mound only two days later to eliminate the division-rival Phillies. The veteran left-hander induced five whiffs on 21 pitches Thursday as he made just his second relief appearance since the 2018 playoffs, when he worked out of the bullpen twice during Boston's World Series run. Even without the relief appearance, Sale would have been on short rest to start Game 1 of the NLDS against the Dodgers on Saturday, which makes him a logical candidate to pitch Sunday in Game 2, especially since that would still him up for a potential winner-take-all Game 5.

item.content:encoded:
Tonight, the Atlanta Braves hosted the Philadelphia Phillies in a one-off game.
It was a highly anticipated division showdown.
The Phillies chose to put Aaron Nola on the mound… and early in the game, he didn't exactly live up to his managers' expectations.
In the first inning, after four batters, the score was 3-0. Michael Harris II hit a three-run homer after his teammates drew two walks.
Nola ended up pitching for less than two innings, even though his last start (which also went poorly) was five days ago. #RegularSeasonBreak
Ray Kerr, meanwhile, was slated to be an opener for the Braves. But he pitched longer than Nola in his first postseason start, thanks in large part to his defense.
The spin throw from Mauricio Dubón
The pick from Matt Olson
What a beautiful play by the @Braves defense! pic.twitter.com/fpAJ8LPwWx
— MLB (@MLB) October 2, 2026
Kerr didn't allow any runs in 3.1 innings of work. He was excellent.
The Phillies, meanwhile, quickly turned to Zack Wheeler. It was the right move, and manager Don Mattingly will have decisions to make if they advance to the Division Series.
The problem for the Phillies? Early in the game, they didn't put themselves in a position to worry about the series against the Dodgers.
Ozzie Albies went 5-0 with a two-run homer.
The Phillies pulled within 5-1, but the Braves maintained their five-run lead as Matt Olson hit a solo home run.
Then, with the score 6-2 and the Phillies gaining momentum, the Braves brought in Chris Sale. This likely makes up for his bullpen session between starts, but will he be able to pitch on Saturday? Sunday?
Sale hadn't pitched in relief in the playoffs since the 2018 World Series.
So the Braves have eliminated the Phillies. They'll face the Dodgers in the Division Series.

item.title: [MLB.com] What's it like to face Miz? We asked those who have
item.dc:creator: Adam McCalvy; Zach Sweet

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE -- To the Twins, it looked like a fastball you could see out of the hand – and then it was past you. To the Rockies, it was a pitch that seemed to reach the plate before they could react. The Braves geared up for 100 mph, then found themselves chasing cutters and sliders.
The Cubs had faced Jacob Misiorowski more than most teams. Their manager still described a fastball at the top of the strike zone that “nobody can hit.” The Phillies came within one Kyle Schwarber swing of literally getting no hits in nine innings.
“You see some guys that throw 103 [mph], but you get a little bit more time. A guy like that, where he's almost dropping it in the catcher's mitt, man, it makes for a tough day,” Judge said in May, after Misiorowski struck out 11 and touched 103.6 mph in his first career start against the Yankees. “I was excited to get a chance to face him and see him for the first time.
“You know, I’ve seen a lot of his games and seen what he's done; it's impressive stuff, man. They've got a great, great, great young star over there.”
Across the league, opponents spent the season looking for an answer when Misiorowski was on the mound. They struggled, as he finished with a 1.80 ERA, 252 strikeouts, a 0.80 WHIP and a .157 opponents’ average, each the best mark in the Majors. He enters October as the clear favorite for the National League Cy Young Award. On Saturday, the Padres will get the next chance when Misiorowski starts Game 1 of the National League Division Series.
Ask the hitters who faced him what makes the assignment so difficult, and velocity is only the beginning.
“Marshy asked me after the game,” said Phillies star Bryce Harper in June, referring to teammate Brandon Marsh, “he's like, ‘That's probably the best guy I've ever faced.’ And he asked me who’s one of the best guys I've ever faced, and I said Matt Harvey. He had that extension heater, and he was one of the first guys that really rode that heater at the top of the zone. Obviously, 104 [mph] is a little bit different.”
That was after Misiorowski’s finest start of the season, a 15-strikeout, 27-batter, 95-pitch shutout in front of a spellbound crowd at American Family Field on June 12, the one-year anniversary of Misiorowski’s Major League debut.
Harper, perhaps with October in mind, saw a silver lining.
“I'm happy we were able to face him – and I'm not saying that in a good way or bad way, but I was just happy we were able to face him and see what that looked like,” he said.
The Twins had their own trouble in an Aug. 9 matchup, when Misiorowski reached 200 strikeouts faster than all but one pitcher in history. Misiorowski began that night by throwing 21 consecutive four-seam fastballs. Royce Lewis saw one at 103 mph in his first at-bat and called it one of the most difficult pitches he had ever faced.
Brooks Lee noticed how far Misiorowski’s 6-foot-7 frame carried him down the mound, and how his position on the first-base side of the rubber changed the angle. Even a hitter who recognized what was coming had little time to do anything about it.
“It comes out of his hand and you feel like you see it well, and then it’s by you,” Twins hitter Kody Clemens said. “Especially up in the zone.
“If he throws a fastball in the upper part of the zone, I feel like it’s damn near impossible to hit.”
Twins manager Derek Shelton pointed to the pitch’s movement near the top of the zone. Hitters had to judge whether it would be a ball or strike while trying to catch up to 100-plus mph. He called it “probably one of the most challenging at-bats in the game.”
“Honestly, we were scratching, clawing, trying to get to him in any way, shape or form,” Colorado outfielder Cole Carrigg said.
Misiorowski threw 66 pitches at 100 mph or harder that day, a single-game record in the pitch-tracking era. Rockies manager Warren Schaeffer saw more than a radar-gun reading.
“That’s a one-of-one fastball, 103 with all that extension,” Schaeffer said. “It’s hard to react to that. And he throws it all the time.”
Against Atlanta in August, the problem changed shape. Misiorowski threw six scoreless innings in a matchup with Chris Sale, a pitcher he grew up admiring. Sale left impressed by “probably the most impressive fastball I’ve ever seen.” Braves manager Walt Weiss explained what happened when hitters prepared for it.
“You’re gearing up for 100, and then you’re having to deal with cutters and sliders,” Weiss said. “It’s among the toughest at-bats.”
The Cubs’ Seiya Suzuki had offered a similar assessment after facing Misiorowski in June, on the night he fired a 105.5 mph fastball against Pete Crow-Armstrong to match the third-fastest pitch since tracking began in 2008.
“Everybody had good swings and good at-bats,” Suzuki said through interpreter Edwin Stanberry, “but overall, he just pitched better.”
The Cubs did find a way through on Sept. 2 at Wrigley Field, scoring five runs in the first two innings and chasing Misiorowski after four while snapping his streak of 25 consecutive outings allowing three or fewer earned runs. Alex Bregman homered on a slider low in the zone and added a two-run single on a 102 mph fastball. Beforehand, Cubs manager Craig Counsell had identified the opening: Get a pitch lower in the zone, because the high fastball was so hard to hit even when hitters expected it.
“When he executes, you’re in trouble,” Counsell said. “That’s generally how the great ones are.”
Six days later, the Cubs saw him again. Misiorowski opened by striking out Crow-Armstrong on a 103.7 mph fastball, reached 104.5 against Suzuki and allowed one run over 6 1/3 innings. Along the way, he threw his 1,000th pitch of the season at 100 mph or harder.
“That’s how I throw,” Misiorowski said afterward. “The guys on the other side expect that.”
They do. By now, hitters from New York to Philadelphia to Minnesota to Colorado to Atlanta to Chicago, and across the entire league, can describe the fastball, the angle and the pitches that follow.
The Padres will arrive with their own plan. Then someone will have to stand in the box and try to make it work. Nobody has consistently done that against the presumptive NL Cy Young winner in 2026.

item.title: [fansided.com] 5 free agent landing spots for Michael King after sterling playoff start
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: The San Diego Padres blitzed the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of the NL Wild Card series, 8-0, to put themselves one win away from a date with the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS. Plenty of Padres deserve credit for Tuesday night's dominant performance, but none more than soon-to-be-free agent Michael King. item.content:encoded:
The San Diego Padres blitzed the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of the NL Wild Card series, 8-0, to put themselves one win away from a date with the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS. Plenty of Padres deserve credit for Tuesday night's dominant performance, but none more than soon-to-be-free agent Michael King.
San Diego's ace put together one of the best postseason starts in recent memory, carrying a no-hitter into the seventh inning. He finished with seven scoreless frames, allowing one hit, three walks and recording eight strikeouts. As Padres fans celebrate King's masterclass, prospective free agency suitors are chomping at the bit. Here are a few potential landing spots:
Atlanta Braves
The Braves rotation is a bit scarce behind Chris Sale. Tyler Mahle has eviscerated the competition since arriving at the trade deadline, but he's a free agent next winter. AJ Smith-Shawver, J.R. Ritchie and Owen Murphy are all exciting young arms, but it's unclear which of them will click as full-time starters — and how soon. Martín Pérez, one of this season's great surprises for Atlanta, is also an upcoming free agent.
Atlanta doesn't typically pay sticker price on free agent pitchers but there is immense pressure to compete now — right now — in the twilight years of Sale's career. He won't be able to anchor this rotation forever and the Braves need to start hedging their bets, just in case Father Time catches up.
King, with a 3.21 ERA and 1.18 WHIP, has made 32 starts and pitched a career-high 185 innings this season. The Braves need depth and dependability most desperately, and that's something King can provide. It doesn't hurt that he is building a nice postseason résumé for himself.
Baltimore Orioles
Every winter, we all wonder if Baltimore might finally upgrade its pitching staff. The Corbin Burnes era burned bright and fast. Shane Baz was a savvy trade addition last winter, but the Orioles still struggled to field five quality, healthy starters for the 162-game duration of the regular season.
Trevor Rogers, their best pitcher two years running, will now enter free agency. That leaves Baltimore's front office will a clear and immediate need in the rotation. It seems like the O's new ownership group will, on some level, spend more than the previous administration. The Pete Alonso signing was a stark departure from business as usual in Baltimore. As such, it's not hard to envision the O's ponying up for a second-tier ace like Michael King; the Tarik Skubals of the world are still outside their price range, no doubt.
If Kyle Bradish can finally get healthy for a year, and if the O's deign to re-sign Rogers (or pursue another mid-rotation arm in addition to King), this rotation could shape up quite nicely. Baltimore has the offensive firepower to compete in the AL East. King can help round out a postseason-caliber roster.
Toronto Blue Jays
A nightmare Blue Jays season has finally come to an end, but Toronto should be right back in the postseason fray next season with better luck and an productive winter. The Jays front office is probably the most aggressive in baseball outside of L.A. or New York.
Last offseason, their big fish was Dylan Cease, who immediately turned in a Cy Young-caliber campaign. At the trade deadline, Toronto did not strictly sell, despite sitting near the bottom of the standings. The Jays went out and added José Soriano, another frontline starter at the peak of his powers.
Toronto can expect a healtheir Trey Yesavage in 2027, too, so a premium free agent addition (like King) could quickly transform the Blue Jays rotation into one of the deepest and most fearsome in the American League. If Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and Toronto's boppers put their best foot forward, there's no reason Toronto can't win the division and compete (again) for a World Series.
Houston Astros
The Astros went bullpen against bullpen in their AL Wild Card series opener against the White Sox. Houston was lucky Chicago only managed six runs, with many, many base-runners stranded in scoring position. That did not mean much for the Astros, unfortunately, as the Chicago bullpen — against all odds — mostly kept a more seasoned Houston lineup in check.
Houston has a proper 1A ace in Hunter Brown, but the rotation behind him is total patchwork. Peter Lambert put together a solid campaign and Ethan Pecko faired well in his first taste of MLB action, but the Astros can't really trust anyone besides Brown. Tatsuya Imai, their prized free agent addition last winter, was little more than a bulk reliever in his rookie season.
The Astros have gotten cheaper and cheaper in recent years and the results are getting worse and worse, predictably. Still, this core has competed for a World Series in the not-so-distant past, and we know ownership is capable of spending at the upper echelon of free agency. King would do a lot to solidify the Astros' pitching plans in 2027.
Chicago Cubs
Injuries decimated the Cubs rotation this season. Justin Steele, Cade Horton and Ben Brown should all return in 2027, which is a major, natural influx of talent. If Edward Cabrera can rebound, the Cubs rotation will be all rainbows and sunshine — at least on paper.
But as this season once again reminded us, what happens "on paper" almost never translates to reality. Shōta Imanaga and Matthew Boyd are both upcoming free agents. Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, Chicago's emergency deadline rentals, are also halfway out the door. There's uncertainty around how exactly the likes of Steele and Horton will perform coming off of major elbow surgeries, too. So the Cubs should play it safe and hyper-focus on pitching depth.
The rotation could be what sends Chicago home against San Diego. So, why not use the Padres own weapons against them in free agency and sign King? "Stability" is a word that comes to mind with King, and that's exactly what the Cubs need right now.

item.content:encoded:
It’s do or die for the Phillies on Wednesday.
The Braves pushed them to the brink in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card with a 5-3 decision prompted by Austin Riley’s three-run shot in the eighth inning.
Another win in this series would mark first time the Braves prevailed over their NL East rivals in the postseason: the Phillies took the NLDS in both 2022 and 2023 and the 1993 NLCS over Atlanta.
This Phillies’ core has been chasing after a World Series throughout the decade, and another early exit will have its ramifications.
The onus to avoid that comes down to no one more than Bryce Harper, who struck out twice and went hitless Tuesday.
Phillies vs. Braves Game 2 prediction, best bet
Harper, who is a .269 postseason hitter in 58 games, narrowly missed a go-ahead two-run home run against Chris Sale in the sixth inning when the ball just sailed just right of the right-field pole.
He gets the lefty vs. righty matchup advantage against Atlanta’s Tyler Mahle, against whom he has posted a healthy .278/.350/.500 slash line.
Mahle leans on his four-seamer for nearly half of his pitches. He doesn’t throw it with extreme movement or overpowering velocity, averaging 92 mph, but he locates the strike zone with it well.
In the 14 four-seamers that Mahle served to Harper this season, Harper knocked two hits with a home run on eight swings, according to Statcast. Only two were whiffs.
In fact, Mahle wasn’t much of a swing-and-miss pitcher at all, ranking in only the 31 percentile.
That’s all while Harper remained an elite contact hitter, posting a .379 xwOBA, a Statcast metric that measures expected offensive production based on the exit velocity and launch angle of his contact rather than the results.
Harper has stated he loves playing at Truist Park, and his numbers say why.

The two-time MVP hit .320 there in 27 plate appearances this season, which included a pair of home runs and five multi-base games out of six.
As the clubhouse leader, Harper was adamant about how the Phillies need to “finish the job” this postseason after having been here before.
He’ll have no choice but to deliver on that statement Wednesday.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] MLB Playoff Roundup: Austin Riley’s blast stuns Phillies
item.dc:creator: Matt Ferenchick
item.description: Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series couldn't have gone much better for the Yankees. On the mound, Cam Schlittler was excellent, blanking the Red Sox for 6.1 impressive innings. Then, led by Ben Rice, the Yankees' offense plated nine runs, pulling away from Boston to go up 1-0 in the series. Yesterday wasn't just the opening of the Yankees-Red Sox series, though. All three of the Wild Card matchups also got underway on Tuesday, so let's check in on what happened. AL Wild Card Series Game 1 Chicago
item.content:encoded:
Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series couldn't have gone much better for the Yankees. On the mound, Cam Schlittler was excellent, blanking the Red Sox for 6.1 impressive innings. Then, led by Ben Rice, the Yankees' offense plated nine runs, pulling away from Boston to go up 1-0 in the series.
Yesterday wasn't just the opening of the Yankees-Red Sox series, though. All three of the Wild Card matchups also got underway on Tuesday, so let's check in on what happened.
AL Wild Card Series Game 1
Chicago White Sox 6, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago leads 1-0)
After jumping out to a 3-0 lead early, the White Sox withstood the Astros and tacked on some more runs late to take the opener of the other AL matchup in Houston.
Facing an Astros' bullpen game, the White Sox got going quickly. With a runner on third in the first, Munetaka Murakami hit a fly ball that was deep enough for Chicago's Sam Antonacci to tag up and score. The next inning, Antonacci did it at the plate, hitting a bases loaded single to bring home two more runs. A Colson Montgomery homer in the fourth and a Chase Meidroth RBI single in the fifth had Chicago up big before Houston showed any resistance.
A two-run shot from Nelson Velázquez in the bottom of the fifth got the Astros on the board, but Chicago got one of those runs back a little while later. Houston countered with one in the eighth and brought the tying run to the plate, but couldn't cash in as the ChiSox held on from there. Amusingly, the Astros have now lost eight consecutive playoff games in Houston since early on in the 2023 playoffs. If Chicago can win one more at Daikin Park either today or tomorrow, they'll not only eliminate Houston but also secure their first playoff series victory since winning the 2005 World Series, over two decades ago. The Astros will have their best pitcher going for them in Hunter Brown, so we'll see if that's enough to keep their season alive.
NL Wild Card Series Game 1
Atlanta Braves 5, Philadelphia Phillies 3
(Atlanta leads 1-0)
Austin Riley's go-ahead eighth inning home run stunned the Phillies to give the Braves the series opener.
The Phillies opened the scoring early when Alec Bohm doubled home a run in the top of the first. Atlanta then answered back with Mike Yastrzemski RBI single. The game remained tied for a while after that as both Chris Sale and Jesús Luzardo put in solid outings; Luzardo hadn't necessarily been expected to even last five innings, as he was still relatively fresh off the IL and threw an inning of relief just to help the Phillies clinch a playof spot on Sunday. Things changed as both teams got to the bullpen, and there were some dramatic swings.
Atlanta took the lead for the first time in the sixth when Ozzie Albies hit an RBI triple thanks to some less-than-stellar fielding from Phillies' center fielder Derek Hill. However, a Ronald Acuña Jr. misplay in the seventh allowed J.T. Realmuto to hit a triple of his own, scoring two runs to put Philly back in front.
Phillies' manager Don Mattingly went for the kill shot by bringing on closer Jhoan Duran in the seventh. He got through that inning fine and came back out for the eighth, facing the heart of Atlanta's order. He got two quick outs before Michael Harris II kept the inning alive with a softly-struck infield single. Duran hit Albies with a pitch after that, bringing Riley to the plate. Duran then left a fastball right in the middle of the zone, and Riley took full advantage, giving Atlanta a lead that Raisel Iglesias held on to in the ninth.
If the Braves win today, then they'll advance to play the two-time defending champion Dodgers in the NLDS. If the Phillies can hold them off behind ace Cristopher Sánchez however, then Game 3 awaits on Thursday.
San Diego Padres 8, Chicago Cubs 0
(San Diego leads 1-0)
Michael King took a no-hitter into the seventh inning as the Padres' offense crushed Cubs pitching in the late night game out west.
The Cubs' story this season is that they have an excellent offense and poor pitching, ranking first and last in fWAR respectively. However in Game 1, only one of those things proved true. Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado both hit first inning home runs against Matthew Boyd, getting San Diego off to the perfect start, from which they only added on to their lead.
Meanwhile, the Cubs offense couldn't do much against King. The former Yankee didn't allow a hit until Nico Hoerner singled with one out in the seventh. In total, King shut out Chicago over seven frames, allowing just the one hit and three walks, striking out eight.
In the ninth inning, Padres' pitcher Joe Musgrove returned to the majors after a two-year absence while recovering from Tommy John surgery. He allowed a couple Cubs to reach base, but did end up throwing a scoreless inning.

item.title: [MLB.com] Riley flips Game 1 with 8th-inning blast on 99.9 mph pitch from Phillies' closer
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: ATLANTA -- Austin Riley supported Chris Sale’s strong start, halted the Phillies’ postseason dominance of Atlanta and put six months of frustration behind him with a swing that could make October worth savoring for both him and the Braves. Riley’s three-run homer off All-Star closer Jhoan Duran with two outs in the eighth inning gave the Braves a thrilling 5-3 win over the Phillies in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon at Truist Park. “I’m happy for Austin Riley,
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Austin Riley supported Chris Sale’s strong start, halted the Phillies’ postseason dominance of Atlanta and put six months of frustration behind him with a swing that could make October worth savoring for both him and the Braves.
Riley’s three-run homer off All-Star closer Jhoan Duran with two outs in the eighth inning gave the Braves a thrilling 5-3 win over the Phillies in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon at Truist Park.
“I’m happy for Austin Riley,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It’s been a tough year for him. But this just goes to show you, when the playoffs start, everything starts at zero. Nothing that happened in the regular season really matters. It’s a clean slate. Austin Riley has been a great postseason player.”
Four of Riley’s six career postseason homers have been of the go-ahead variety and three of those have been hit in the eighth inning or later. That eighth inning or later total matches Troy Glaus, Bernie Williams, Jose Altuve and Freddie Freeman for the most in MLB history.
The slugging third baseman previously hit a go-ahead shot in the ninth inning of Game 1 of the NLCS on Oct. 12, 2020, and he hit a go-ahead two-run home run with two outs in the bottom of the eighth in Game 2 of the 2023 NLDS, also against the Phillies. Chipper Jones is the only other Braves player with multiple go-ahead homers in the eighth inning or later of a postseason game.
“I know how my season went,” Riley said. “It’s not the way I wanted it to. But that's the beauty of the postseason. You get a clean slate and go out there and try to do something for the boys and for this city.”
Instead of talking about being on the brink of elimination, the Braves joyfully discussed how everything changed when Riley sent Duran’s 99.9 mph fastball over the right-center-field fence for a go-ahead home run.
Riley doesn’t remember what any of his teammates said after he returned to a jubilant dugout after his home run. Was he also in a haze as he rounded the bases?
“I remember my gum falling out of my mouth,” Riley said.
It was a jaw-dropping moment that put the Braves in an encouraging position.
In the history of the best-of-three Wild Card Series, teams taking a 1-0 lead have gone on to win the series 21 of 24 times (88%), including 17 two-game sweeps. Home teams have won all nine series in which they have gone ahead 1-0, including eight sweeps.
The Phillies had won six of the previous eight postseason games played against the Braves this decade. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 2022 and ‘23 NL Division Series.
“It doesn't get more fun than this, playing this game in the postseason,” Weiss said. “You can imagine going from losing the lead to something like that. The swinging emotions are enormous. What a big home run.”
Sale played a significant role in this crucial Game 1 victory. The Braves ace registered nine strikeouts over 6 1/3 innings. Two of the three runs he surrendered came via a J.T. Realmuto triple that Didier Fuentes surrendered with two outs in the seventh.
So where was Sale when the value of his strong effort was preserved by Riley’s home run?
“I was getting some arm care in, and unfortunately the [clubhouse] TV I was watching was on the delay [feed],” he said. “I just heard craziness coming from the entire clubhouse. Everyone's losing their mind, and I'm just sitting there like, ‘Oh, what's going on?’ About four seconds later, you see what happened. I just couldn't be happier for him.”
Coming off two injury-shortened seasons, Riley hit .219 with 19 homers and a .654 OPS during the regular season. Safe to say this was the most frustrating season of the two-time All-Star’s career. This past weekend in Miami, he talked about how relaxing his right shoulder might have helped him hit two homers in last week’s Reds series.
The triple came against a 98.2 mph splitter that was in the middle of the zone. The ball had 109 mph exit velocity and it traveled a Statcast-projected 394 feet.
This home run came against a 99.9 mph four-seamer that was middle in. This is the hardest-thrown pitch Riley has homered against in his career, besting a homer he hit against Jacob deGrom’s 99.7 mph heater on July 1, 2021.
This latest home run had a 104.6 mph exit velocity and it traveled a projected 385 feet.
It would have been a home run in 27 of 30 MLB ballparks. Did Riley know it was gone?
“No, I did not,” he said. “I was just praying as I was running to first.”

item.content:encoded:
Chris Sale struck out nine over 6 1/3 innings while allowing three runs in a no-decision versus the Phillies on Tuesday in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series.

Sale allowed just one run while he was in the game, but a pair scored in the seventh after he exited on a two-run triple by J.T. Realmuto. The left-hander was so much better than this line suggests while generating 22 swings-and-misses with 16 of those coming on his slider. Sale remains one of the best starters in baseball — although with more volatility because of durability at age 37 — and if Atlanta can’t come from behind and win, he’ll be the ace of the staff again to start 2027.

In the NLWC series opener against the Phillies, Austin Riley will bat seventh and play third base, which isn't a huge surprise.
Here is the full Atlanta Braves batting order, per @UnderdogMLB:
"Braves 9/29 D. Baldwin C R. Acuña Jr. RF M. Olson 1B M. Dubón LF M. Harris II CF O. Albies 2B A. Riley 3B M. Yastrzemski DH H. Kim SS C. Sale SP"
A few lineup notes: Mike Yastrzemski gets the start at DH, with the anticipation that Luzardo won't throw very long, and Ha-Seong Kim gets the start at SS. Mauricio Dubon is the team's cleanup hitter, and Ozzie Albies (who crushes lefties) will bat sixth.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Quietly Cut Ties with 27-Year-Old Player Before Phillies Playoff Series
Looking at Austin Riley's 2026 Season
Now that the regular season is officially in the books, we can take a look at Austin Riley's season as a whole.
Over 159 games played and 566 total at-bats, Austin Riley batted .219 with 19 home runs and a career-low OPS+ of 80.
He also added 21 doubles, 72 RBI, 64 runs scored, and 124 hits to the Braves' regular-season offense.
However, the regular season is in the past, and Austin Riley can write all those wrongs by having a big moment or two in the MLB playoffs. Riley would likely be the first to admit he had a poor offensive season, but October baseball can bring a breath of fresh air to players who struggled over the past several months.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Receive Clarity on Phillies' Pitching Plans Ahead of Wild Card Series
